# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Critical reading: the strongest evidence in the series, but the main follow-up numbers have unresolved problems

This report directly answers questions the earlier papers left open, using a randomised design, record-based output, a second hours measure and a pre-registered mediation test. The headline result is a per-hour gain of **8.5% (3.4 to 13.8)** at 24 months. That is credible, and it settles one argument: the gain is not "entirely an artifact".

However, an unreported contamination of the control group, a mismatch between the hours measure and the meetings mechanism, and some overclaiming affect how the main findings should be read.

## Arithmetic check

- **Output per hour:**
  - Timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098, so **+9.8%**.
  - System logs: 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085, so **+8.5%**.
  - Halden subset: 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, a fall of 13.4%; 96.8 / 86.6 → **+11.8%**.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **Counter-office staffing:** output per FTE fell 11.4%, so restoring it needs 1 / 0.886 ≈ 13% more staff, close to the county's 12%. A 9% rise in cost per contact is plausible if staff are about three-quarters of costs, but it's an estimate.

## What the report settles

- **The re-analysis's "entirely an artifact" claim is refuted.** The 24-month estimate meets every standard Varga and Holm recommended, and its interval clearly excludes zero.
- **The meta-analysis's "no decay" claim is undermined.** The four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, exactly as I suspected, so they cannot speak to decay.
- **Coverage-bound work is resolved in practice.** The county ended the counter arm. Restoring service would need about 12% more staff at higher cost per contact.
- **The meeting data now include a baseline.** Treated offices started at 7.4 hours a week and controls at 7.2, so the month-6 gap was not there before the trial. That answers a concern I raised about the nine-month report.

## Problems

### 1. Control-group contamination affects the decay estimate

Two of the seven control offices cut their meetings in month 15. They then gained **4.1% in output per hour**. The report treats this as a side observation, but it changes the comparison.
- Two of seven controls improving by about 4% raises the control average by roughly 1.2%, for months 15–24.
- That alone could account for part of the measured fall from 12.5% to 9.8%. Some of the "decay" may be the controls getting better, not the treatment fading.
- The 24-month gain is therefore probably *understated* relative to an uncontaminated control group.

The report should give estimates that exclude the two offices, or that are restricted to months before 15.

The averages also look odd. If the two offices stayed at 5.0 hours of meetings, the control average of 7.0 at month 24 implies the other five rose from about 7.2 to about 7.8. That should be checked.

### 2. The decline is not statistically tested

The claim that the gain "declined by about a quarter" compares two point estimates. Their intervals overlap almost completely: +6.9 to +18.4 at nine months against +4.6 to +15.2 at 24 months. The report correctly criticises the meta-analysis for asserting no decay without a within-study test, then asserts decay without one itself.

The fair statement is narrower. The data are consistent with modest fading, possibly partly caused by the contamination in point 1, and *inconsistent* with fading to zero.

### 3. The log-hours measure doesn't fit the meetings mechanism

The logs record active time on the **case-management system**. That is not a stricter measure of total working time. It is a different and narrower measure, which presumably leaves out meetings, email and phone work.

This matters for the mediation analysis:
- **If meetings are outside log time,** cutting them can't remove low-value hours from the denominator. That was the nine-month report's mechanism. The mediation result would then have to mean that fewer meetings make case time more productive, for example through less interruption. That is a different claim, and the report doesn't distinguish the two.
- **The numbers don't obviously reconcile.** Starting from 37.9 hours, a 12% fall leaves about 33.4. Meetings fell by about 3.3 hours relative to control. So *non-meeting* time fell by only about 1 hour, roughly 3–4%. Yet log time fell 11%. Either a lot of non-meeting work is off-system, or staff count as logged in during meetings. The paper needs to say which.
- **On that rough arithmetic, meetings could explain almost the whole gain.** Output per non-meeting hour would have risen only about +0.5% (0.966 / 0.96). That would support the meetings mechanism *more* strongly than 47%. It depends on details the paper doesn't give, so it should be verified rather than relied on.

### 4. "Confirms" overstates the mediation test

- **It uses the same offices.** The hypothesis came from the 7 treated case-processing offices, and the "confirmatory" test uses the same 7 offices, over a period that includes the months that generated the hypothesis. Registering before outcomes are known is good practice. This is still not an independent replication.
- **There are still only 14 offices.** A "larger sample of office-months" adds repeated measures, not independent units. A 47% (28 to 66) interval looks narrow for 14 clusters, and the paper doesn't say how correlation within offices over time was handled.
- **The mediators are confounded.** Meetings and fatigue are probably linked: fewer meetings may themselves reduce fatigue. How the shared effect is assigned between them changes the 47/18 split. The limitations section notes the confounding assumption, but the Summary still says "confirms".

"Strongly supports" would be accurate. "Confirms" is not.

### 5. Cost in case-processing is still missing

The report gives cost per contact for the counter arm. It doesn't give the same figure for case-processing, the arm being continued. Staff kept full pay while output per FTE fell 3.4%, so cost per case rose by at least about 3.5%, plus any paid overtime. For a county deciding whether to keep the schedule, that is the deciding number.

### 6. Halden follow-up: smaller points

- **The reversion description is stretched.** "All with client-facing or coverage obligations" includes a marketing agency that cited **client deadlines**. That is deadline-bound, discretionary work under the meta-analysis's own coding. One of the three reversions is therefore in the category where the schedule is supposed to work.
- **There is another layer of selection.** Only 14 of 23 organisations replied, on top of the attrition and continuation selection the report already notes.
- **There is no allowance for the trend.** A comparison with a pre-pilot baseline about 2.5 years earlier picks up normal productivity growth and any changes to the business. "Upper bound" is the right description, but the report doesn't say what it is bounding against.

### 7. Smaller points

- **Sick days** (−27%) are still not adjusted for fewer scheduled days. This is the third paper in a row not to do so.
- **Appeal overturn rates** (3.2% v 3.0%) are more meaningful at 24 months, because more appeals have now been decided. They still have no confidence interval.
- **The meeting-audit offices** add two cases with no comparison group, compared against their own earlier months, which may also reflect regression to the mean. The authors' own caveats are appropriate.
- **The authors are judging their own work.** The authors are evaluating their own hypothesis, and one co-author led the Halden pilot whose critics this report rebuts. That doesn't invalidate the results, but it makes the overclaims in the Summary more notable.

## Where the five papers now leave the question

- **Coverage-bound work:** reduced hours cut output per worker by about 11% and worsened service. Keeping service needs about 12% more staff. The one randomised employer stopped it.
- **Discretionary work:** a gain of roughly **8–10% per actual hour** lasts at least two years in one randomised setting. Output per worker sits about 3% below control. Cost per unit of output rises modestly, though no paper reports it.
- **Decay:** modest at most, and possibly overstated here because of control contamination. A collapse to zero is ruled out.
- **Mechanism:** cutting meetings is now the leading explanation, more important than reduced fatigue. The key open question is still the one the authors raise: can reorganisation alone capture most of the gain, or does the hours cut make it happen? Answering it needs a trial with a "reorganise without cutting hours" arm.
